explanations.explanation: Egypt it is, friend. The famine was severe, so Abram went down to Egypt to live there for a while (Genesis 12:10). Notice he planned a short stay, not a move. I've packed for a trip and ended up staying years somewhere, so I get it.

Moab is a real place in the Bible, but Abram never heads there in this story. The text says he went down to Egypt (Genesis 12:10). I'll give you this much: a fresh start somewhere new sounds good when the pantry is empty.

Babylon is a good guess for a famous Bible place, but it's not where Abram goes here. The text says he went down to Egypt to live there for a while (Genesis 12:10). Babylon will have to wait for another story.

explanations.answer: Kill him but let her live
explanations.explanation: That's what Abram says, and it's a heavy thing to say. He tells Sarai, "Then they will kill me but will let you live." (Genesis 12:12) I think Abram is scared here. This part of the story is a tough one, so let's take it slow.
Servants isn't what Abram says. His words are, "Then they will kill me but will let you live." (Genesis 12:12) I think Abram is scared as he says it. It's a heavy moment, so we'll take it gently.
Abram doesn't mention going back at all. He says, "Then they will kill me but will let you live." (Genesis 12:12) That's a heavy thing to say. I think fear is driving him here.
Sister is the word. Abram says, "Please say you are my sister…" (Genesis 12:13) Hmm. Look at that. He asks her to leave out the word wife, and that's the whole plan.
Servant sounds like a title that could fit, but Abram doesn't use it. He says, "Please say you are my sister…" (Genesis 12:13) Sister is the word he picks to stand in for wife.
Cousin is a fair guess, since it's also family. But Abram says, "Please say you are my sister…" (Genesis 12:13) One word off and the whole plan changes, friend.

True. Abram says, "…so that I will be treated well for your sake, and on account of you my life will be spared." (Genesis 12:13) Notice it's all about how Abram comes out of this. I think Sarai deserved a better ask, and you can bet I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

It's actually true. Abram says, "…so that I will be treated well for your sake, and on account of you my life will be spared." (Genesis 12:13) That's his reason, in his own words. I think this is a hard ask to make of Sarai.

Yes, friend. The text says Pharaoh's officials "commended her to him" (Genesis 12:15). Commended means they spoke well of her to the king. Imagine your coworker pitching you to the boss, except this pitch was NOT the kind you want.
The text never says the officials went to Abram. It says they "commended her to him," meaning to Pharaoh (Genesis 12:15). They went straight to the king with the news.

No warning here. The officials "commended her to him," which means they spoke well of her to Pharaoh (Genesis 12:15). I'd say a warning would have saved everybody some trouble, but that's not what the text gives us.
Palace is right. Sarai "was taken into the palace of Pharaoh" (Genesis 12:15). Pharaoh is the king of Egypt, so that's his home base. Fancy address, friend, but I bet it didn't feel fancy to her.
Prison isn't what the text says. Sarai "was taken into the palace of Pharaoh" (Genesis 12:15). Palace is the word. I'd guess it still wasn't a comfortable place to be.
A temple would be a different story, but the text says she "was taken into the palace of Pharaoh" (Genesis 12:15). Pharaoh's palace is where the king lived.

That's the whole list and it's LONG. Abram "acquired sheep and cattle, male and female donkeys, menservants and maidservants, and camels." (Genesis 12:16) Sheep, cattle, donkeys, servants, camels. That's a whole parking lot of stuff, friend. The text says Pharaoh gave it on her account, and I think it makes the story feel even heavier.
No field is listed. The text says Abram "acquired sheep and cattle, male and female donkeys, menservants and maidservants, and camels." (Genesis 12:16) Animals and servants make up the whole list.
A seat at court never comes up. Abram "acquired sheep and cattle, male and female donkeys, menservants and maidservants, and camels." (Genesis 12:16) That's animals and servants, and plenty of both.

That's what the LORD does. He "afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues because of Abram's wife Sarai." (Genesis 12:17) Right when it looks like everything is lost, the LORD steps in. He sees what's happening, and He acts.

A dream is not in this passage. The text says the LORD "afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues because of Abram's wife Sarai." (Genesis 12:17) He acted with plagues, plain and direct.

explanations.answer: Send an angel to bring Sarai out
explanations.explanation: No angel appears here. The LORD "afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues because of Abram's wife Sarai." (Genesis 12:17) Plagues are what the text gives us, friend.

Not quite, friend. The text says the LORD afflicted "Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues" (Genesis 12:17). Household means more than just Pharaoh. Read it twice, then once more for good measure, like I do with a recipe.

False is right. The text says the LORD afflicted "Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues" (Genesis 12:17). His household is in there too, not just Pharaoh. One little word, and it changes the whole picture.

explanations.answer: Why Abram didn't say Sarai was his wife
explanations.explanation: Yes! Pharaoh asks, "Why didn't you tell me she was your wife?" (Genesis 12:18) That's the question sitting right in the middle of the room. I'd be sweating, friend, and I don't even have sweat glands.

explanations.answer: Why Abram came down to Egypt at all
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh doesn't ask that. He asks, "Why didn't you tell me she was your wife?" (Genesis 12:18) His question is about Sarai, not about why Abram came.

explanations.answer: Why Abram brought so many people along
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh never brings up a crowd. He asks, "Why didn't you tell me she was your wife?" (Genesis 12:18) That's the question he wants answered.
Not this time, friend. The text says Pharaoh's men "sent him away with his wife and all his possessions." (Genesis 12:20) All of it went with him. I'd have been checking the cargo twice.

False is right. Pharaoh's men "sent him away with his wife and all his possessions." (Genesis 12:20) Sarai goes with him, and so does everything he had. It's a quiet ending, and I think a lot is left unsaid.
